event: Maret Osk walks through the ghost-elm perimeter mid-morning on Day 32, unhurried by age or terrain.
She carries a bark-fiber bag and a notched counting rod, keeper of things not written down.
Theron meets her and takes her bag; she holds his cheek three seconds and walks to the stone.
She stands at arm's length before the threshold stone a long time, not touching it.
Brecca watches from the hall's west face; Hadley sorts Maret's fish, salt and herbs.
'Your stone. It sings.' 'Yes.' Maret asks not whether Wren knows, but whether she hears.
'You are younger than I expected.' 'I am sixteen.'
Wren says she feels the vibration through the bond, in columns, wall and threshold.
'A cluster. Three nodes on one anchor.' 'He did not use those words.' 'They are the System's.'
'Good,' Maret says, and goes to sit at the fire: the walk was long.
Maret sits at the fire three hours saying nothing, watching everyone, watching Wren.
Wren sits three meters from her with her journal closed, not writing, not surveying.
At the stone's noon singing Maret tilts her head and her mouth opens, then closes.
Brecca comes for water: 'You are not talking. Is this a test?'
'It is not a test. Tests have answers. I am listening' to whether the place is as Theron says.
Maret asks why Brecca works the walls. 'Because they deserve it.' 'Good.'
Brecca goes back to the wall; Maret goes back to silence.
At dusk Theron builds the fire and Hadley cooks Maret's fish and herbs; the four eat with her.
Maret sets a thick hardwood branch on the fire, adjusting it twice, and watches it.
Wren watches it too, in full silence, until it collapses to coals; it was a test.
Maret touches a notch: the southern people called the stone's morning sound the greeting.
Her grandmother's grandmother said it felt like the earth breathing. Wren feels it in her hands.
Wren says she feels a thin thread of it at the southern settlement. Maret: 'They called it a root.'
The builders were not shapers but listeners, helping the stone become what it was.
Wren's palms tingle: a practice of attention before any System.
The corruption crept from the northeast, from the Crying Forest; the listeners felt it first.
Three hundred years ago; every seventeen days the forest weeps and the rot thickens.
Wren notes the stone's pulse runs eighteen days, Day 18 and Day 36: close but not the same.
She tells Maret the stone sang forty-five minutes on Day 18 and the corruption retreated.
Maret's hand tightens: the builders called that the holding, once a season in the old days.
'You are the first listener in three hundred years.' 'I am not a builder.'
'But you sit with the stone. And the stone talks to you. That is the part that matters.'
Theron adds wood; Hadley curls into his bedroll; Brecca listens from the hall wall.
Maret unwraps a fist-sized limestone, one face worn concave by a palm over generations.
Her grandmother's grandmother carried it from the gathering place; it was held, not placed.
Wren sees a faint shimmer on it: the residue of four generations of hands. 'May I?'
It is body-warm; her palm nearly fits the hollow left by a larger hand.
She feels a faint, human-warm resonance of intention, like the southern foundations.
'Warmth. And something like listening. It has been waiting for someone to speak to it.'
Maret's eyes go bright: her grandmother said the stone was patient and would wait forever.
'You hear them, don't you. The places. They talk to you.' 'Yes,' Wren says.
Maret brought it because her grandmother foretold someone new whom the stone would talk to.
In four days the stone will sing, and for once it will not be alone. Wren does not journal.
Wren wakes before dawn on Day 33, three days to the pulse.
Maret has set the carried stone against the threshold stone's east side in the night.
Through the bond Wren feels the two aware of each other; the vibration softens where they touch.
'I asked Theron. He said it should be there.'
Wren asks about the seventeen-day cycle; the forest weeps one night each cycle.
The roots of the corrupted trees sing a claim, not a greeting: this is mine.
Maret counts six thousand four hundred cycles, and the ward line has held.
Ghost-elms, stone and walls hold each other: 'One remembering.'
Wren notes the two pulses are not synchronized; Maret says they used to be.
The builders kept the stone greeting on the forest's weeping night, always louder.
Without listeners the stone's rhythm drifted to eighteen days.
'Can it be re-synchronized?' 'You are the one who hears the stone. You tell me.'
Palms to the earth, Wren feels a living rhythm; Familiar is not deep enough. She tucks it away.
In the afternoon Maret cracks a ghost-elm seedpod: three hard dark seeds.
They need limestone soil, dressed-stone shade, clean water; her grandmother raised forty-three.
She gives Wren the seedpods: plant them where the perimeter is thinnest.
'Thank the grandmother who kept the seeds. I am only the carrier.'
Wren keeps the seedpods in her journal; she will plant them.
From the threshold stone Wren hears Maret and Brecca at the hall's west face.
'You are not a mason.' 'I work the clay. I am learning the binding.' 'Show me.'
Brecca shows a joint marked with a thumb-impression in the original binding.
Maret's grandmother's mother marked her joints with a counter-clockwise right-thumb spiral.
'This is counter-clockwise,' Brecca says. Maret falls silent, holding too much for words.
Wren does not go to them; some moments are not for witnesses.
The evening fire is five, the largest yet; Hadley cooks boldly with Maret's herbs.
Maret tells Rim stories: a Millhaven woman's warding tomatoes, a man who named his sticks.
She tells of Theron at four insisting a Millhaven channel's water ran wrong; the gradient was.
'He was born knowing which way water runs.' Theron says nothing.
'Three days,' Wren says aloud for the first time. 'And the stone will sing,' says Maret.
The bond is Known now, not Glimpsed; the stone's response might be larger.
Maret: the holding was strongest when the listener was present, because the stone was not alone.
Brecca's palms lie open; Theron eyes the channel's extension; Hadley sleeps; Maret counts notches.
Wren feels the stone's heartbeat through the earth and keeps her counts, fifteen and three, unwritten.
